name: Offline RL and Conservative Q-Learning (CQL / IQL / TD3+BC)
key_paper: Kumar et al., 'Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning', NeurIPS 2020. Also: Kostrikov et al., 'Offline Reinforcement Learning with Implicit Q-Learning (IQL)', ICLR 2022. Fujimoto & Gu, 'A Minimalist Approach to Offline Reinforcement Learning (TD3+BC)', NeurIPS 2021.
algorithm_description: Offline RL trains a policy entirely from a fixed, pre-collected dataset without any online environment interaction. Conservative Q-Learning (CQL) adds a regularization penalty to the standard Bellman update that minimizes Q-values for out-of-distribution (OOD) actions and maximizes Q-values for actions in the dataset, preventing overestimation of unseen action combinations. IQL avoids querying Q-values for unseen actions altogether by using expectile regression on in-dataset action values only. TD3+BC adds a behavior-cloning regularization term directly to the policy gradient, penalizing deviation from the logged behavior policy. All three variants can be applied to a fixed historical dataset without needing to interact with the environment, making them uniquely suited to settings where data collection is constrained (e.g., one draw per week in lottery).
action_space_handling: Standard CQL/IQL/TD3+BC are designed for continuous action spaces, but discrete-action CQL exists and is well-documented. For the lottery combinatorial case (select k from N), the action space is exponentially large (~C(50,7) ~ 99M for LottoMax). In practice, the Q-function must either (a) output a scalar Q-value for a given (state, action) pair where action is a multi-hot vector, or (b) be factored autoregressively across ball positions. Option (a) is simpler to implement given the existing transformer architecture. TD3+BC is most straightforwardly adapted because it treats the actor as a constrained imitation of the behavior policy.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: Within offline RL the actor (policy network) generates the combinatorial output; the Q-function (critic) scores it. The actor can produce a probability distribution over {1..N} and then apply top-k sampling, Gumbel-top-k, or autoregressive masking to form an exactly-k-distinct set. CQL/IQL score this set as a whole via Q(s, a). Alternatively, the actor can generate a multi-hot logit vector and the critic can score the softmax-normalized version. During training the conservative penalty is applied at the set level. No pointer-network or flow-based sampling is built into the offline RL framework; those are choices for the actor architecture operating inside the offline RL training loop.
sequential_generation_strategy: Offline RL imposes no specific generation strategy — it wraps any actor architecture. The actor inside CQL/IQL/TD3+BC can be flat multi-hot (jointly sampled k numbers from a multi-label softmax), autoregressive (one number at a time conditioned on previous choices), or flow-based. For lottery-nn, the most natural fit is to reuse the existing SharedLotteryTransformer as the actor and add a separate critic network. Joint flat multi-hot output is the easiest path; autoregressive would add the ability to model inter-number correlations but requires significant additional architecture work.
gradient_estimator_type: In offline RL, the actor is typically trained by maximizing Q(s, pi(s)) with a straight backpropagation through the actor (if the action is continuous or differentiably sampled). For discrete/combinatorial actions, a Gumbel-softmax / straight-through estimator is needed to differentiate through the argmax or top-k operation. TD3+BC avoids this entirely by adding a BC term that directly imitates logged actions (supervised loss), which is fully differentiable. IQL avoids actor gradients through Q entirely — it trains the actor with advantage-weighted regression (AWR), which uses REINFORCE-style weighting with dataset actions, avoiding the need to sample new actions at all.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: The offline RL framework does not itself enforce combinatorial constraints — that is delegated to the actor. During policy improvement, CQL maximizes Q(s, a) over the action space which for exponentially large discrete sets requires either (a) enumerating a random subset of candidates and taking the argmax (approximate), (b) using Gumbel-top-k sampling to select exactly k balls differentiably, or (c) autoregressive masking where each step conditions on previously selected numbers to prevent repetition. IQL with advantage-weighted regression (AWR) avoids this problem by only using dataset actions — the constraint is enforced at data collection time. For lottery-nn, IQL+AWR is the safest path since the dataset actions (historical draws) are already valid k-distinct sets.
sample_efficiency_rating: medium — Offline RL methods were designed for large offline datasets (thousands to millions of transitions in robotics, Atari, etc.). With fewer than 200 draws, the conservative Q-value penalty in CQL needs careful calibration: too strong and the critic learns to assign low Q-values everywhere; too weak and Q-value overestimation returns. IQL is more forgiving because it never queries OOD actions during training. TD3+BC is the most sample-efficient of the three because the BC term provides a strong supervised signal even with minimal data. Sample efficiency is medium rather than high because Q-function learning with sparse rewards (most lottery plays score 0) is inherently data-hungry.
regularization_built_in: CQL: explicit conservative penalty (subtracted softmax Q term over the action space); optional entropy term for the policy. IQL: expectile regression implicitly prevents Q overestimation; advantage-weighted regression clips large advantages via temperature parameter beta. TD3+BC: behavior cloning term lambda * BC_loss added to policy gradient, normalized by mean absolute Q-value to balance scales. All three benefit from standard weight decay and dropout applied to actor/critic networks. For small datasets, the BC component in TD3+BC and the advantage clipping in IQL provide the most meaningful regularization.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: 1. Q-value collapse: with fewer than ~50 non-zero reward samples, the critic may converge to near-zero Q-values everywhere, making policy gradient steps uninformative. 2. Distribution mismatch amplification: CQL penalizes OOD actions which with very few data points means nearly all reasonable plays are penalized. 3. Sparse reward propagation failure: if fewer than ~10 plays in the dataset have any hit (reward > 0), temporal difference updates cannot reliably propagate signal. 4. Overfitting critic: a separate critic network trained on 100-200 samples will overfit its Q-estimates even with regularization. 5. TD3+BC degenerates to pure BC: if the Q-signal is too noisy, the BC term dominates and the method collapses to imitation learning with no RL improvement.
data_regime_evidence: Minimum training samples tested: The original CQL paper uses D4RL datasets with thousands to hundreds of thousands of transitions. IQL similarly uses large offline datasets (HalfCheetah, Hopper: ~1M transitions). TD3+BC uses 1M-transition D4RL datasets. No major offline RL paper as of 2025 has formally validated these methods on fewer than 200 samples. The closest evidence comes from: (1) Decision Transformer applied to Atari with 1% data regime (~50K transitions, still >> 200); (2) offline RL for medical treatment with ~500-1000 patient records. Performance degradation curve: extrapolating from published ablations, CQL degrades significantly below ~1000 samples; IQL degrades below ~500; TD3+BC (with strong BC regularization) is most graceful, but its Q-critic likely becomes unreliable below ~200 samples. Comparison baseline: all three outperform behavior cloning on large datasets, but at very small n the advantage over BC shrinks substantially. [uncertain]
convergence_guarantees_small_n: CQL has finite-sample bounds (Kumar et al. 2020 Theorem 3.3) showing that the conservative penalty ensures the learned policy's value is lower-bounded by the dataset behavior policy's value — but these bounds scale with dataset size n as O(1/sqrt(n)), implying high uncertainty at n=100-200. IQL has no published finite-sample theory as of 2025. TD3+BC has no formal convergence theory. In practice, convergence at n<200 is empirically uncertain for all three methods, particularly with sparse rewards. [uncertain]
reward_distribution_handling: All three methods handle sparse reward via temporal difference propagation — Q-values for states preceding successful plays should accumulate positive signal. However, with lottery's ~95% zero-reward plays, the Q-function is effectively learning from a nearly-all-zeros reward signal over 100-200 samples. Distributional extensions (C51, QR-DQN) can be added to any of these methods to model the full return distribution rather than just the mean, which is beneficial for risk-sensitive play generation. Minimum draws needed for stable Q-learning: estimated 500+ for reliable signal propagation, though IQL+AWR may work with ~200 if the reward is semi-bandit (per-number hits counted rather than play-level only). The semi-bandit formulation (credit assignment at number level) is critical to making offline RL viable at n<200.
credit_assignment_granularity: By default, offline RL assigns reward at the play level (did the set of k numbers match?). This is the coarsest possible assignment and wastes the signal from partial matches. For lottery-nn, the reward should be redesigned as number-level semi-bandit feedback: reward_i = 1 if number i in the play appeared in the actual draw, else 0. This gives k signals per play instead of 1, effectively multiplying the usable reward signal by k=7. IQL with AWR can incorporate this naturally by treating each number selection as a separate action with its own advantage estimate. CQL requires a factored Q-function to support this. TD3+BC can use a per-number loss in the BC term weighted by per-number reward.
diversity_mechanism: None of the three methods have built-in diversity mechanisms for play generation at inference time. Options: (1) temperature scaling on the actor's output logits before top-k sampling; (2) entropy bonus in the policy objective (SAC-style), though adding this to CQL requires care to avoid destabilizing the conservative penalty; (3) IQL with AWR naturally introduces some diversity through the advantage-weighted sampling — actions with positive advantage are preferred but not deterministically selected. For multiple plays per prediction call (lottery-nn generates 5 plays per call), an explicit diversity reward or a repulsion mechanism between generated plays must be added separately.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: Fully offline — this is the defining property of the CQL/IQL/TD3+BC family and the primary reason they are relevant here. All three methods train exclusively from a fixed historical dataset with no environment interaction required. This is the correct RL paradigm for lottery: with one draw per week, any online RL method that requires thousands of environment steps is operationally impractical. The dataset is simply the historical draw CSV (draws.csv, draws_649.csv, draws_dailygrand.csv). After each new weekly draw, the dataset is augmented by one sample and the model can be retrained offline. This aligns perfectly with the existing `main_swarm.py joint-train` workflow.
complexity: medium — IQL and TD3+BC are simpler to implement than CQL. Adding a critic network (separate from the actor) and a modified training loop to existing lottery-nn is moderately complex. The main challenge is adapting the combinatorial action space.
key_dependencies: PyTorch only (all three methods are implementable in pure PyTorch). Optional: `d3rlpy` library (Python, PyPI) provides production-quality implementations of CQL, IQL, and TD3+BC with minimal glue code. `tianshou` also has offline RL support. No additional heavy dependencies beyond what lottery-nn already uses.
estimated_lines_of_code: IQL: ~200-300 lines (critic network + expectile loss + AWR policy update). TD3+BC: ~150-200 lines (add BC term to existing actor training). CQL: ~250-350 lines (critic + conservative penalty). Shared scaffolding (replay buffer, offline training loop): ~100 lines common to all.
transfer_learning_compatibility: High — all three methods separate the actor (policy network) from the critic (value network). The existing SharedLotteryTransformer can serve directly as the actor; only a new critic network needs to be added from scratch. The actor weights are initialized from the pretrained swarm checkpoint (models/best_swarm.pt) and fine-tuned via the offline RL objective. This is one of the strongest arguments for offline RL in this project: the existing 253K-parameter pretrained backbone is not wasted, unlike methods that require training from scratch.
specific_application_in_project: Offline RL (specifically IQL or TD3+BC) would replace the current temperature-softmax sampling in `src/predict.py` with a principled policy optimization loop. The actor remains the SharedLotteryTransformer; a new critic MLP is added (input: state embedding from transformer, output: scalar Q-value). Training uses the historical draws CSV as a static offline dataset. Reward is semi-bandit (per-number hit count) to maximize credit assignment at n<200. After each weekly draw, the dataset grows by one sample and `joint-train` is extended to also run the offline RL update. IQL is recommended first (simpler, no OOD action queries, most robust at small n); TD3+BC is the fallback if IQL's Q-signal is too noisy. CQL is a Phase 3 candidate once more data accumulates. Integration target: all three lotteries via the swarm's per-lottery heads, with a shared critic backbone analogous to the shared actor backbone.
replaces_or_extends: Extends — adds a Critic network and offline RL training loop alongside the existing SharedLotteryTransformer Actor. The temperature-softmax sampling at inference time is replaced by policy network sampling guided by the learned Q-function. The existing `joint-train` command is extended with an offline RL update step.
existing_open_source_implementations: 1. `d3rlpy` (GitHub: takuseno/d3rlpy) — production-quality Python library with CQL, IQL, TD3+BC, SAC, BCQ, BEAR; integrates with PyTorch; actively maintained as of 2025. 2. `CORL` (GitHub: tinkoff-ai/CORL) — clean single-file offline RL implementations of IQL, TD3+BC, CQL, DT in PyTorch. 3. Official CQL implementation: GitHub stevenygd/CQL (older). 4. `tianshou` offline RL module. 5. IQL reference implementation: GitHub ikostrikov/implicit_q_learning. 6. TD3+BC reference: GitHub sfujim/TD3_BC. D3rlpy and CORL are the most practical for integration.
benchmark_results: CQL (D4RL benchmark, NeurIPS 2020): achieves 44.0 normalized score on hopper-medium vs 29.0 for BC baseline; 72.5 on walker2d-medium vs 75.3 BC — competitive with or better than BC on most tasks. IQL (ICLR 2022): 47.4 on hopper-medium-v2 vs 52.5 CQL; achieves state-of-art on antmaze tasks (antmaze-large-diverse: 58.6 vs CQL 12.5). TD3+BC (NeurIPS 2021): 59.3 on hopper-medium vs 42.6 BC; competitive with CQL with significantly less code. All results on datasets with >> 200K transitions — direct small-data comparison not available in published literature.
notable_use_cases: 1. Offline RL for medical treatment policies (sepsis, ICU ventilation) — fixed historical patient records, sparse reward, no online interaction — structurally similar to lottery (fixed dataset, cannot run new experiments). 2. Recommendation systems trained offline from logged user interactions — combinatorial item selection, sparse click reward, large action spaces. 3. Autonomous driving policy learning from demonstration datasets (CARLA, nuScenes). 4. Chip placement (Google, Nature 2021) uses a related offline RL approach on fixed simulation data. The medical and recommendation-system use cases are the most structurally analogous to lottery: fixed dataset, sparse reward, combinatorial action space.
